section.title: Wound-Rotor Motors: Construction, Resistance and Torque

previousOverview: Original Zack Hartle ID/media/progress retained in its existing stable section, now optional further study. New core section contains exactly the two requested videos.

videos.title: Wound-Rotor Motors: Construction, Operation and Starting
videos.teaches: Wound stator/rotor, insulated slip rings, brushes, external resistor bank, starting sequence, high-torque applications, resistance speed control and losses, open-circuit and brush/connection faults.
videos.flow: Construction and cage comparison → induced rotor current → application → starting and speed control → equipment and maintenance. Explicitly refers learners to the supplied resistance/current/torque sequel.

ranges.topic: Starting, resistance controllers and speed control

videos.limits: Simplified torque/PF claims are not universal. The closing claim that these motors cannot reverse is too broad: suitability depends on motor, brush gear and drive design. A single open connection does not prove all rotor currents and torque are zero. The 50% slip example is not a universal speed range. Caption review is not visual confirmation of every diagram.
videos.qualification: Reduce rotor resistance as speed rises. Reversal depends on the motor and brush-gear design; wound-rotor motors are not universally non-reversible. Rotor-circuit faults can reduce torque or prevent starting; isolate before inspection.

videos.title: Wound-Rotor Motors: Rotor Resistance, Current and Torque
videos.teaches: Slip speed, rotor speed/EMF/frequency/reactance, R/X/Z and in-phase rotor current; compares low-resistance cage, high-resistance cage and adjustable-resistance wound rotors.
videos.flow: Defines every table column before comparing three rotors; concludes with resistance reduction maintaining high starting/accelerating torque. Follows construction and basic slip/torque lessons.
videos.limits: The 0.707 rotor-PF condition is an approximate rotor-only-model result, not a general stator supply power factor or universal full-equivalent-circuit result. Constant torque/current relies on the illustrated resistance schedule and model assumptions. The 60 Hz, 1800 rpm and 6 V examples are data, not local installation ratings; automatic captions obscure some decimal values.
videos.qualification: The 0.707 rotor power factor and constant-torque table describe a simplified model, not universal motor limits. Examples use 60 Hz; rotor frequency equals slip multiplied by supply frequency.

technicalSources.supports: Full T equivalent circuit includes stator/leakage/magnetising terms; rotor-only simplifications are conditional.
